Content: "debilitating cognitive function later in life" -my dad is a big football fan, And I frequently watch games with him, and now I can't help but notice the really bad decisions by players on the field. Author: @antistarlet
Content: Very well researched video. As a neuroradiologist, I find the rates of CTE in professional sports people incredibly concerning and for me, the evidence for CTE in American football is unequivocal. I'm based in the UK so we don't play much American football but there has been a number of dementia diagnoses in former football (soccer) players. It seems that "heading" heavy leather footballs back in the 70s and 80s probably resulted in the accumulation of small, possibly subclinical, concussions. On a separate but related note, there has also been a number of relatively young former professional rugby players (both union and league) who have been diagnosed with MND (ALS) in recent years. No evidence that there's a definite link at this stage (pending ongoing research) but it's definitely worrying to find potentially another neurodegenerative process occuring in professional sportsmen. I'm convinced that, in time, contact sports like rugby will no longer be viable commercially due to the correlation with significant cognitive decline and there will be a corresponding dropoff in numbers, which it seems is already the case with American Football. Similar to Flag Football, there's been an uptick in Tag rugby which is the non-contact version at the grassroots level. Anyone who's interested in Mike Webster's story, the discovery of CTE and the NFL's response should read the excellent book "League of Denial" by Mark Fainaru-Wada.

Author: @jojodelacroix
Content:
Just wanted to add that concussions on kickoffs are back up this year. They were largely down because kickers were kicking the ball out of the endzone. But that's not happening anymore, so with more returns being made, more players are being injured. I'm not exactly sure why since there is the shorter distance being covered. It could be a difference in strategy or perhaps most of the injuries are being incurred by returners. I'm not sure. But I do know that there's be a noted, very large uptick in concussions and other injuries this year on kickoffs. Looks like the NFL is going to need to go back to the drawing board again.

It's also worth noting that Kickoffs are considered special teams. And many players that are part of special teams aren't stars, but rather edge of the roster players that are considered special teams specialists. These players get paid far less than star players, often the league minimum (which can be under a million dollars). They are less likely to suffer brain injuries from repeated hits if they're not playing a lot of offense or defense, but they are in on the highest risk plays (ie kickoff returns) which means they are more likely to end up getting major injuries. Ones that are both debilitating AND which end their career.

Author: @silvers983
Content: Anecdotes have limited usefulness obviously, but I can say for a fact that I was at least mildly concussed WAY more often than I ever wanted to let on when I played Texas HS football. I wasn't a good player, never even played varsity level, and I was getting many of the symptoms I was being asked about by athletic trainers. I just lied. This is a huge component that I think people underestimate. There are severe concussions that you can't hide, but mild concussion symptoms are almost entirely dependent on self reporting. You can't tell that someone has a headache, that the classroom lights are too bright and painful sometimes, or that someone's brain feels a little foggier than usual. Not unless they tell you. In football culture, at least in Texas HS football culture, reporting these symptoms was made out to be a big sin. You were letting your teammates down. You just wanted to get out of practice or hard work. You were just weak. So of course, as a testosterone fueled 16 year old boy, you'd sooner die on the field before admitting those symptoms. More than 10 years removed, with social capital no longer on the line, I can definitively say that my cognitive ability before football vs after were vastly different, and my mental health overall was markedly worse. I played for a total of 4 years. I can't imagine the damage the players that play for decades at much, much higher levels than I ever did have accumulated.

Author: @Arthur3148
Content:
Here in Europe, rugby faced a similar concussion problem. Drastic changes were implemented. Now in pro games there is an independent doctor who can ask for a player to go off field, be replaced, and pass a concussion protocol to determine if he's fit to go back to play. And players wear a connected mouth guard which measures the power of head impacts they take and can also trigger a concussion protocol. If a player has too many concussions, he also can be prohibited to play for a given time. And the rules have changed, with harsher penalties against players who make tackles which can endanger the tackled player (making him fall on his head, neck or shoulders, head to head or shoulder to head contact, uncontrolled/dangerous tackles, etc). 

Then, in its spirit, American football is different because it allows almost every type of tackling and you can tackle almost any player at any time (in rugby you only can tackle the player with the ball and you have to grab them under the waist). And the fact they wear heavy protection gear like big helmets and body armour might also give the players a false sense of safety and induce more dangerous tackles. So regulating the tackling might alter the spirit of the game, but I think they should implement the concussion protocols.

Content: Pro and college football players are professional warriors who are in the business of being injured for fame, glory and fortune, and "CTE" is not a "sacred holy victim baby" category of injury.
